To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we propose a model-free de-biasing procedure that is easy to implement, and the proposed procedure can be applied to a variety of clinical trials.

we propose a new method for inference on a selected subgroup that is model-free, asymptotically sharp, and easy to compute, that we demonstrate its merits by reanalyzing a clinical trial, and that we show that the method of subgroup selection post hoc should be considered when performing a subgroup analysis.

we develop a de-biased bootstrap inference procedure to evaluate the subgroup effect of a selected subgroup in clinical trials and that our proposed method is model free, easy to compute and asymptotically optimal, and it is shown to outperform the existing methods in the MONET1 clinical trial.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a statistical analysis of selected subgroups in clinical trials, and our goal is to address the question of what is the best selected subgroup and to evaluate how good the best selected subgroup really is.
the problem of statistical inference for the best selected treatment effect in clinical trials, which can be applied to the analysis of subgroup effects.
the following question: How should we analyze a selected subgroup in a clinical trial?

the proposed de-biasing method is an effective way to correct for the bias in the subgroup effect estimation and the proposed bootstrap method is an effective method to construct a valid confidence interval for the subgroup effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a new method for subgroup analysis in clinical trials, and we demonstrate the importance of subgroup analysis in clinical trial data analysis.
, if we are interested in the effect of the treatment for a selected subgroup, we should first address how the subgroup is chosen and then use our proposed method to de-bias the subgroup effect.
we have proposed a new method that allows one to make valid statistical inferences for a selected subgroup effect in a clinical trial, even when the subgroup is not selected independent of the data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
when a subgroup is selected based on the observed data, the subgroup effect should be evaluated with a bias-corrected estimate.
when we select a subgroup after observing the clinical trial data, the subgroup effect estimate may be biased and the usual confidence interval is too short.
the statistical evaluation of a selected subgroup should not be performed as if the subgroup is chosen independently of the data.
